# Introduction

This example shows how to apply the quality control (QC) of rFILTER to PM<sub>2.5</sub> observations from a network of low-cost sensors. The QC tests are applied step by step, in the order of the FILTER methodology:

- Range Validity: `range_validity_qctest()`
- Constant Value: `constant_value_qctest()`
- Outlier Detection: `outlier_qctest()` and `spatial_outlier_qctest()`
- Spatial Correlation: `spatial_correlation_qctest()`
- Spatial Similarity: `spatial_similarity_qctest()`

Finally, the individual flags are combined into a total quality flag with `quality_flag_function()`. The detailed description of each test is given in its help page (e.g., `?spatial_correlation_qctest`).

The example uses two of the sample datasets included in rFILTER:

- `network_sensor_data`: hourly PM<sub>2.5</sub> observations from a network of low-cost sensors, which are quality controlled.
- `reference_data`: hourly PM<sub>2.5</sub> observations from reference stations, used as high-quality neighbors in the Spatial Correlation and Spatial Similarity tests.

# Load the package and the datasets

```{r, include = FALSE}
# packages used only for the tables, charts and maps of this example
library(tidyr)
library(leaflet)
library(leaflet.minicharts)
library(highcharter)
library(htmlwidgets)
```

```{r}
library(rFILTER)
library(dplyr)

# load the sensor and reference datasets
data("network_sensor_data")
str(network_sensor_data)

data("reference_data")
str(reference_data)
```

Both datasets share the same structure: the location identifier (`id`), its coordinates (`longitude` and `latitude`), the timestamp (`timestamp`) and the PM<sub>2.5</sub> concentration. The concentration is stored in `PM2.5` for the sensors and in `value` for the reference stations.

The map below shows the locations of the sensors and the reference stations.

```{r, echo = FALSE, out.width = "100%"}
sensor_info <- network_sensor_data %>%
  distinct(id, longitude, latitude)

reference_info <- reference_data %>%
  distinct(id, longitude, latitude)

leaflet(width = "100%", height = 450) %>%
  addProviderTiles("Esri.WorldTopoMap") %>%
  addCircleMarkers(data = sensor_info,
                   lng = ~longitude, lat = ~latitude,
                   popup = ~paste("<b>Sensor:</b>", id),
                   stroke = TRUE, color = "#eb6834", radius = 7, fillOpacity = 0.9) %>%
  addCircleMarkers(data = reference_info,
                   lng = ~longitude, lat = ~latitude,
                   popup = ~paste("<b>Reference station:</b>", id),
                   stroke = TRUE, color = "#2a78d6", radius = 7, fillOpacity = 0.9) %>%
  addLegend(position = "topright", colors = c("#eb6834", "#2a78d6"),
            labels = c("Low-cost sensors", "Reference stations"),
            title = NULL, opacity = 0.9)
```

The figure below shows the time series of the raw PM<sub>2.5</sub> observations of each sensor, before QC.

```{r, echo = FALSE, out.width = "100%"}
highchart(type = "stock") %>%
  hc_add_series(data = network_sensor_data,
                hcaes(x = datetime_to_timestamp(timestamp), y = PM2.5, group = id),
                type = "line") %>%
  hc_yAxis(title = list(useHTML = TRUE, text = "PM<sub>2.5</sub> (&mu;g m<sup>-3</sup>)"),
           opposite = FALSE) %>%
  hc_tooltip(useHTML = TRUE, headerFormat = NULL,
             pointFormat = "<b>Sensor {series.name}</b><br>{point.x:%Y-%m-%d %H:%M}<br>PM<sub>2.5</sub>: {point.y:.1f} &mu;g m<sup>-3</sup>") %>%
  hc_legend(enabled = TRUE,
            layout = "vertical", align = "right", verticalAlign = "top",
            maxHeight = 300,
            navigation = list(enabled = TRUE)) %>%
  hc_size(height = 450)
```

# Quality control

The QC consists of the following tests, applied in this order.

## Range Validity

- **Purpose:** checks whether observations lie within physically realistic limits. The limits are set with the `upper.bound` and `lower.bound` arguments.
- **Flag:** `flag_range`
  - `0`: invalid (out of range)
  - `1`: valid (within range)

For more information, see `?range_validity_qctest`.

```{r, eval = TRUE}
sensor_qc_data <- range_validity_qctest(data = network_sensor_data,
                                        data.column = "PM2.5",
                                        upper.bound = 1000,
                                        lower.bound = 0,
                                        new = FALSE,
                                        param = "PM2.5")

# count of each flag value (0 = out of range, 1 = within range), including NA
table(factor(sensor_qc_data$flag_range, levels = c(0, 1),
             labels = c("0: out of range", "1: within range")), useNA = "always")
```

## Constant Value

- **Purpose:** checks whether the values remain constant (flatline behavior) within a temporal window. The window and the sensitivity of the test are set with the `persist.duration`, `compl.persist.duration` and `min.variation` arguments.
- **Flag:** `flag_constant_value`
  - `0`: invalid (insufficient data)
  - `1`: invalid (constant)
  - `2`: valid (not constant)

For more information, see `?constant_value_qctest`.

```{r, eval = TRUE}
sensor_qc_data <- constant_value_qctest(data = sensor_qc_data,
                                        date.column = "timestamp",
                                        data.column = "PM2.5",
                                        id.column = "id",
                                        persist.duration = 8,
                                        compl.persist.duration = 6,
                                        method = "range",
                                        min.variation = 0.1,
                                        new = FALSE,
                                        param = "PM2.5")

# count of each flag value (0 = insufficient data, 1 = constant, 2 = not constant), including NA
table(factor(sensor_qc_data$flag_constant_value, levels = c(0, 1, 2),
             labels = c("0: insufficient data", "1: constant", "2: not constant")), useNA = "always")
```

## Outlier Detection

- **Purpose:** checks for abnormal values (outliers) within a temporal window. The test is performed in two steps, each with its own function:
  - `outlier_qctest()`: checks each sensor independently, without considering its neighbors. The window and the sensitivity of the test are defined through `outlier.duration`, `compl.outlier.duration` and `outlier.threshold`.
  - `spatial_outlier_qctest()`: evaluates the measurements flagged as outliers in the previous step by looking at the wider neighborhood. The neighborhood, with its inner and outer radii in km, is defined through `outlier.radii`, and the number of neighboring sensors required to confirm whether a value is an outlier is given by `outlier.minneigh`.

  With this approach, erroneous outliers flagged by `outlier_qctest()` can be distinguished from real abnormal events (e.g., a pollution episode observed by several nearby sensors).

- **Flag:** `flag_outlier`
  - `0`: invalid (insufficient data)
  - `1`: invalid (outlier)
  - `2`: valid (not an outlier)

For more information, see `?outlier_qctest` and `?spatial_outlier_qctest`.

```{r, eval = TRUE}
# temporal outlier detection
sensor_qc_data <- outlier_qctest(data = sensor_qc_data,
                                 date.column = "timestamp",
                                 data.column = "PM2.5",
                                 id.column = "id",
                                 outlier.duration = 168,
                                 compl.outlier.duration = 60,
                                 outlier.threshold = 10,
                                 new = FALSE,
                                 param = "PM2.5")

# count of each flag value (0 = insufficient data, 1 = outlier, 2 = not an outlier), including NA
table(factor(sensor_qc_data$flag_outlier, levels = c(0, 1, 2),
             labels = c("0: insufficient data", "1: outlier", "2: not an outlier")), useNA = "always")

# spatial outlier detection
sensor_qc_data <- spatial_outlier_qctest(data = sensor_qc_data,
                                         date.column = "timestamp",
                                         data.column = "PM2.5",
                                         out.flag.column = "flag_outlier",
                                         id.column = "id",
                                         x.column = "longitude",
                                         y.column = "latitude",
                                         outlier.radii = c(3, 30),
                                         new = FALSE,
                                         param = "PM2.5")

# count of each flag value after the spatial check, including NA
table(factor(sensor_qc_data$flag_outlier, levels = c(0, 1, 2),
             labels = c("0: insufficient data", "1: outlier", "2: not an outlier")), useNA = "always")
```

Before moving to the spatial tests, the results of the Range Validity, Constant Value and Outlier Detection tests are summarized below. For each test, a measurement is counted as valid, invalid, or without data. The last row shows the measurements that passed all three tests.

```{r, echo = FALSE}
qc_three_steps_summary <- bind_rows(
  tibble(test = "Range Validity",    valid = sensor_qc_data$flag_range == 1),
  tibble(test = "Constant Value",    valid = sensor_qc_data$flag_constant_value == 2),
  tibble(test = "Outlier Detection", valid = sensor_qc_data$flag_outlier == 2),
  tibble(test = "All three tests",   valid = sensor_qc_data$flag_range == 1 &
                                             sensor_qc_data$flag_constant_value == 2 &
                                             sensor_qc_data$flag_outlier == 2)
) %>%
  mutate(status = case_when(is.na(valid) ~ "No data", valid ~ "Valid", TRUE ~ "Invalid"),
         status = factor(status, levels = c("Valid", "Invalid", "No data")),
         test = factor(test, levels = unique(test))) %>%
  count(test, status, .drop = FALSE) %>%
  group_by(test) %>%
  mutate(percent = round(100 * n / sum(n), 1)) %>%
  ungroup()

# table: number (and percentage) of measurements per test and status
qc_three_steps_summary %>%
  mutate(value = paste0(n, " (", percent, "%)")) %>%
  dplyr::select(test, status, value) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = status, values_from = value) %>%
  knitr::kable(col.names = c("Test", "Valid", "Invalid", "No data"))
```

```{r, echo = FALSE, out.width = "100%"}
# bar chart: share of measurements per test and status
hchart(qc_three_steps_summary, "bar", hcaes(x = test, y = percent, group = status, n = n)) %>%
  hc_plotOptions(bar = list(stacking = "normal")) %>%
  hc_colors(c("#2a78d6", "#eb6834", "#b4b2a9")) %>%
  hc_xAxis(title = list(text = NULL)) %>%
  hc_yAxis(title = list(text = "Share of measurements (%)"), max = 100) %>%
  hc_tooltip(pointFormat = "{series.name}: <b>{point.y:.1f}%</b> ({point.n} measurements)") %>%
  hc_size(height = 350)
```

## Spatial Correlation

- **Purpose:** checks whether a sensor is correlated with its neighboring sensors and, if provided, reference stations. The correlation is evaluated in one of two ways:
  - over the entire measurement period (`historical = FALSE`): the correlation is computed once, and the resulting quality flag is assigned uniformly to all the measurements of the sensor;
  - within moving temporal windows (`historical = TRUE`): the test runs every day at 23:00 over the preceding `ndays` days, and the resulting quality flag is assigned to the measurements of that day. This gives a time-varying evaluation, at the cost of a considerably longer computation time.

  The neighborhood is defined by an inner and an outer radius, in km, through `corr.radii`, and `compl.corr.threshold` sets the data completeness required within each window or over the entire period. The correlation between a sensor and a neighbor is considered sufficient if it exceeds the threshold given by `expected_correlation()`. A sensor is considered correlated with its neighbors if either of the following holds:
  - at least one neighbor with a sufficient correlation lies within the inner radius, or
  - at least `minneigh` neighbors with a sufficient correlation lie within the outer radius.

- **Flag:** `flag_correlation`
  - `0`: invalid (insufficient data)
  - `1`: invalid (isolated sensor)
  - `2`: invalid (not correlated)
  - `3`: valid (correlated)

For more information, see `?spatial_correlation_qctest` and `?expected_correlation`.

::: {.important}
In this example, which follows the FILTER workflow, `spatial_correlation_qctest()` uses only the measurements that passed the previous QC tests.
:::

```{r, eval = TRUE}
sensor_qc_data <- sensor_qc_data %>%
  mutate(PM2.5_flagged = ifelse(flag_range == 1 & flag_constant_value == 2 & flag_outlier == 2, PM2.5, NA))

sensor_qc_data <- spatial_correlation_qctest(data = sensor_qc_data,
                                             date.column = "timestamp",
                                             data.column = "PM2.5_flagged",
                                             id.column = "id",
                                             id.target = NULL,
                                             rdata = reference_data,
                                             rdata.column = "value",
                                             rid.column = "id",
                                             x.column = "longitude",
                                             y.column = "latitude",
                                             compl.corr.threshold = 60,
                                             corr.radii = c(3, 30),
                                             minneigh = 2,
                                             historical = TRUE,
                                             ndays = 7,
                                             new = FALSE,
                                             param = "PM2.5")

sensor_qc_data <- sensor_qc_data %>%
  dplyr::select(-PM2.5_flagged)

# count of each flag value (0 = insufficient data, 1 = isolated sensor, 2 = not correlated, 3 = correlated), including NA
table(factor(sensor_qc_data$flag_correlation, levels = c(0, 1, 2, 3),
             labels = c("0: insufficient data", "1: isolated sensor", "2: not correlated", "3: correlated")),
      useNA = "always")
```

## Spatial Similarity

- **Purpose:** checks whether a sensor is similar to its nearest reference stations within a temporal window. The neighborhood is defined through `similarity.radii`, and `compl.similarity.threshold` sets the data completeness required within each window. The similarity between a sensor and a neighboring reference station is considered sufficient if it meets the threshold given by `expected_similarity()`. A sensor is considered similar to its neighbors if it shows sufficient similarity to at least one reference station within the neighborhood.
- **Flag:** `flag_similarity`
  - `0`: invalid (insufficient data)
  - `1`: invalid (isolated sensor)
  - `2`: invalid (not similar)
  - `3`: valid (similar)

For more information, see `?spatial_similarity_qctest` and `?expected_similarity`.

::: {.important}
In this example, which follows the FILTER workflow, `spatial_similarity_qctest()` uses only the measurements that passed all the previous QC tests, including `spatial_correlation_qctest()`.
:::

```{r, eval = TRUE}
sensor_qc_data <- sensor_qc_data %>%
  mutate(PM2.5_flagged = ifelse(flag_range == 1 & flag_constant_value == 2 & flag_outlier == 2 & flag_correlation == 3, PM2.5, NA))

sensor_qc_data <- spatial_similarity_qctest(data = sensor_qc_data,
                                            date.column = "timestamp",
                                            data.column = "PM2.5_flagged",
                                            id.column = "id",
                                            rdata = reference_data,
                                            rdata.column = "value",
                                            rid.column = "id",
                                            x.column = "longitude",
                                            y.column = "latitude",
                                            similarity.radii = 30,
                                            similarity.duration = 168,
                                            compl.similarity.threshold = 60,
                                            new = FALSE,
                                            param = "PM2.5")

sensor_qc_data <- sensor_qc_data %>%
  dplyr::select(-PM2.5_flagged)

# count of each flag value (0 = insufficient data, 1 = isolated sensor, 2 = not similar, 3 = similar), including NA
table(factor(sensor_qc_data$flag_similarity, levels = c(0, 1, 2, 3),
             labels = c("0: insufficient data", "1: isolated sensor", "2: not similar", "3: similar")),
      useNA = "always")
```

The results of all QC steps are summarized below. For the spatial tests, measurements that did not pass the previous steps are also counted as no data.

```{r, echo = FALSE}
qc_spatial_steps_summary <- bind_rows(
  tibble(test = "Range Validity<br>Constant Value<br>Outlier Detection",
         valid = sensor_qc_data$flag_range == 1 &
                 sensor_qc_data$flag_constant_value == 2 &
                 sensor_qc_data$flag_outlier == 2),
  tibble(test = "Spatial Correlation", valid = sensor_qc_data$flag_correlation == 3),
  tibble(test = "Spatial Similarity",  valid = sensor_qc_data$flag_similarity == 3)) %>%
  mutate(status = case_when(is.na(valid) ~ "No data", valid ~ "Valid", TRUE ~ "Invalid"),
         status = factor(status, levels = c("Valid", "Invalid", "No data")),
         test = factor(test, levels = unique(test))) %>%
  count(test, status, .drop = FALSE) %>%
  group_by(test) %>%
  mutate(percent = round(100 * n / sum(n), 1)) %>%
  ungroup()

# table: number (and percentage) of measurements per test and status
qc_spatial_steps_summary %>%
  mutate(value = paste0(n, " (", percent, "%)")) %>%
  dplyr::select(test, status, value) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = status, values_from = value) %>%
  knitr::kable(col.names = c("Test", "Valid", "Invalid", "No data"))
```

```{r, echo = FALSE, out.width = "100%"}
# bar chart: share of measurements per test and status
hchart(qc_spatial_steps_summary, "bar", hcaes(x = test, y = percent, group = status, n = n)) %>%
  hc_plotOptions(bar = list(stacking = "normal")) %>%
  hc_colors(c("#2a78d6", "#eb6834", "#b4b2a9")) %>%
  hc_xAxis(title = list(text = NULL)) %>%
  hc_yAxis(title = list(text = "Share of measurements (%)"), max = 100) %>%
  hc_tooltip(pointFormat = "{series.name}: <b>{point.y:.1f}%</b> ({point.n} measurements)") %>%
  hc_size(height = 350)
```

## Total quality flag

- **Purpose:** combines the results of the five individual tests, Range Validity (`flag_range`), Constant Value (`flag_constant_value`), Outlier Detection (`flag_outlier`), Spatial Correlation (`flag_correlation`) and Spatial Similarity (`flag_similarity`), into one total quality flag for each measurement.
- **Flag:** `quality_flag`
  - `2`: high quality (passed all five tests: `flag_range` = `1`, `flag_constant_value` = `2`, `flag_outlier` = `2`, `flag_correlation` = `3` and `flag_similarity` = `3`)
  - `1`: good quality (passed the first four tests, but not the Spatial Similarity test: `flag_range` = `1`, `flag_constant_value` = `2`, `flag_outlier` = `2`, `flag_correlation` = `3` and `flag_similarity` = `0`, `1`, `2` or missing)
  - `0`: other quality (all remaining measurements)

For more information, see `?quality_flag_function`.

```{r, eval = TRUE}
sensor_qc_data <- quality_flag_function(data = sensor_qc_data,
                                        data.column = "PM2.5",
                                        qcflags = c("flag_range", "flag_constant_value",
                                                    "flag_outlier", "flag_correlation",
                                                    "flag_similarity"))

# count of each flag value (0 = other, 1 = good, 2 = high), including NA
table(factor(sensor_qc_data$quality_flag, levels = c(0, 1, 2),
             labels = c("0: other", "1: good", "2: high")), useNA = "always")
```

The table and the bar chart show the number and share of measurements for each value of the total quality flag.

```{r, echo = FALSE}
flag_levels <- c("No data",  "Other", "Good", "High")
flag_colors <- c("#b4b2a9","#eb6834", "#8fbce8", "#2a78d6")

sensor_flags <- sensor_qc_data %>%
  mutate(quality = case_when(quality_flag == 2 ~ "High",
                             quality_flag == 1 ~ "Good",
                             quality_flag == 0 ~ "Other",
                             TRUE ~ "No data"),
         quality = factor(quality, levels = flag_levels))

quality_summary <- sensor_flags %>%
  count(quality, .drop = FALSE) %>%
  mutate(percent = round(100 * n / sum(n), 1))

# table: number (and percentage) of measurements per total quality flag
quality_table <- knitr::kable(quality_summary,
                              col.names = c("Quality flag", "Measurements", "Share (%)"))

# bar chart of the table results
quality_chart <- hchart(quality_summary %>% mutate(color = flag_colors),
                        "column", hcaes(x = quality, y = percent, color = color, n = n)) %>%
  hc_xAxis(title = list(text = NULL)) %>%
  hc_yAxis(title = list(text = "Share of measurements (%)"), max = 100) %>%
  hc_tooltip(headerFormat = "<b>{point.key}</b><br>",
             pointFormat = "{point.y:.1f}% ({point.n} measurements)") %>%
  hc_legend(enabled = FALSE) %>%
  hc_size(height = 300)
```

::::

The bar chart below shows the share of each quality flag for every sensor, sorted from the highest to the lowest share of high-quality data. Use the scrollbar to see all sensors.

```{r, echo = FALSE, out.width = "100%"}
per_sensor <- sensor_flags %>%
  count(id, quality, .drop = FALSE) %>%
  group_by(id) %>%
  mutate(percent = round(100 * n / sum(n), 1)) %>%
  ungroup()

sensor_order <- per_sensor %>%
    dplyr::filter(quality == "High") %>%
    arrange(desc(percent)) %>%
    pull(id) %>%
    as.character()

hchart(per_sensor %>% mutate(id = factor(as.character(id), levels = sensor_order)),
       "bar", hcaes(x = id, y = percent, group = quality, n = n)) %>%
    hc_plotOptions(bar = list(stacking = "normal")) %>%
    hc_colors(flag_colors) %>%
    hc_xAxis(title = list(text = "Sensor ID"),
             min = 0, max = min(9, length(sensor_order) - 1),
             scrollbar = list(enabled = TRUE)) %>%
    hc_yAxis(title = list(text = "Share of measurements (%)"), max = 100) %>%
    hc_tooltip(pointFormat = "{series.name}: <b>{point.y:.1f}%</b> ({point.n} measurements)") %>%
    hc_size(height = 450)
```

The map shows the distribution of the total quality flag at each sensor location. Click a sensor to see its numbers.

```{r, echo = FALSE, out.width = "100%"}
pie_data <- per_sensor %>%
  mutate(id = as.character(id)) %>%
  pivot_wider(id_cols = id, names_from = quality, values_from = n,
              values_fill = 0, names_sort = TRUE) %>%
  left_join(sensor_info %>% mutate(id = as.character(id)), by = "id")

# popup in the same layout as the default one, with black labels
popup_html <- sapply(seq_len(nrow(pie_data)), function(i) {
  counts <- unlist(pie_data[i, flag_levels])
  rows <- sprintf(
    "<tr><td style='text-align:right; font-weight:bold; color:#222; padding-right:8px;'>%s :</td><td style='text-align:right;'>%d</td></tr>",
    flag_levels, counts)
  paste0("<h3 style='margin:0 0 6px 0;'>", pie_data$id[i], "</h3>",
         "<table>", paste(rows, collapse = ""), "</table>")
})

leaflet(width = "100%", height = 450) %>%
  addProviderTiles("Esri.WorldTopoMap") %>%
  addCircleMarkers(data = reference_info,
                   lng = ~longitude, lat = ~latitude,
                   popup = ~paste("<b>Reference station:</b>", id),
                   color = "#000000", radius = 3, fillOpacity = 0.9) %>%
  addMinicharts(lng = pie_data$longitude, lat = pie_data$latitude,
                type = "pie",
                chartdata = as.matrix(pie_data[, flag_levels]),
                colorPalette = flag_colors,
                width = 22,
                layerId = as.character(pie_data$id),
                popup = popupArgs(html = popup_html),
                legendPosition = "topright")
```
